stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before photomechanical reproduction, a popular engraving was often printed from several identical copper plates, since a single plate wore down after a few thousand impressions. Collectors can sometimes tell these duplicates apart: the plates, each cut by a different journeyman in the publisher's workshop, betray ______ separate origins in tiny variations, such as a cross-hatched shadow with one more line than the others.
explanation: Start with the subject of the main clause after the colon. It is "the plates," and its verb is "betray." The phrase "each cut by a different journeyman in the publisher's workshop" interrupts to describe the plates, but it is not the subject. Because "the plates" is plural and the blank needs a possessive (the origins belong to the plates), you need the plural possessive determiner "their." The plural "separate origins" fits this too: several plates have several origins.

A.why: You probably remembered the rule that "each" is always singular, or you matched the blank to "workshop," the singular noun closest to it. But "each" is only part of an interrupting phrase. The subject that does the betraying is "the plates," which is plural, so the singular "its" doesn't match.

C.why: "It's" means "it is," so the sentence would read "betray it is separate origins," which doesn't work grammatically. It is also singular, while the antecedent "the plates" is plural. You likely chose it because it sounds like the possessive "its."

D.why: You got the number right, since the antecedent is plural, but "they're" means "they are." That gives "betray they are separate origins," which puts a second subject and verb in a place that needs a possessive. Read aloud it sounds like "their," and that sound is the trap.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A booster shot works because the first dose leaves something behind. After the initial exposure, most of the B cells that responded die off, but a reserve of memory B cells persists. When the booster arrives, this reserve, already enriched for cells whose receptors fit the vaccine's antigen, outnumbers the naive cells that answered the first dose, and ______ antibodies bind the antigen far more tightly.
explanation: The antibodies belong to the subject of the clause, "this reserve," which also goes with the verb "outnumbers." "Reserve" is a singular noun. It names one group, even though that group is made of many cells. The singular verb "outnumbers" confirms this. The blank needs a possessive, so you need the singular possessive determiner "its."

A.why: You may have found the right antecedent, "this reserve," and then thought of it as "a reserve of memory B cells," which feels plural. Or you may have matched the blank to one of the plural nouns that get in the way: "cells," "receptors," or "naive cells." But the noun the pronoun refers to is "reserve," which is singular. That is why the verb is "outnumbers" and not "outnumber."

B.why: "It's" has the right number, but it means "it is." That gives "and it is antibodies bind the antigen," which adds a subject and verb that don't fit. You likely chose it because it sounds the same as the possessive "its."

D.why: This choice has two errors. "They're" means "they are," so it isn't a possessive. It is also plural, but the antecedent "this reserve" is singular. You may have been drawn in by the plural nouns near the blank and by the fact that it sounds like "their."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Two federal surveys supply most of what economists know about pay in the gig sector. When app-based driving took off in the 2010s, however, neither of the surveys, which between them interviewed more than 60,000 rideshare and delivery workers a year, revised ______ definition of a “full-time worker,” leaving researchers to compare drivers who wait hours between fares with salaried employees as though the two jobs were alike.
explanation: The blank refers to the subject of the main clause. Cross out the prepositional phrase “of the surveys” and the relative clause “which between them interviewed…workers,” and you are left with “neither…revised ______ definition.” Neither is always singular, so you need a singular possessive determiner. That is “its,” not the contraction “it's.” The plural nouns all around it (two surveys, 60,000 workers) are there to pull you toward a plural.

A.why: You matched the pronoun to “surveys” or “workers,” the plural nouns closest to the blank. The real antecedent is “neither,” which is singular even when it picks from a group of two.

C.why: You read it aloud and it sounded right. But “it's” means “it is,” and “revised it is definition” drops a verb where a possessive belongs.

D.why: “They're” means “they are,” so it puts a verb where a possessive belongs. It is also plural, and “neither” is singular.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sealed beneath the collapsed dome of a clay oven at a Bronze Age settlement in present-day Hungary, the lentils that archaeobotanist Réka Fehér recovered there in 2019 kept ______ shape through a lucky accident: the dome fell in while the fire was still smoldering, cutting off the oxygen supply, so the seeds were charred rather than burned to ash.
explanation: The opening modifier (“Sealed beneath…Hungary,”) describes the noun right after the comma, which is “the lentils.” That is the subject of “kept.” The relative clause “that archaeobotanist Réka Fehér recovered there in 2019” is an interrupter. Lentils are plural things, so you need the plural possessive determiner “their.”

A.why: You matched the pronoun to a singular noun from the opening phrase, such as the dome, the oven, or the settlement. That phrase only describes the subject. The subject itself is the plural “lentils.”

B.why: You took Fehér, the noun right before the verb, as the antecedent. She only appears inside the relative clause. It was the lentils that kept their shape, not the archaeobotanist.

C.why: You got the number right but picked the contraction. “They're” means “they are,” and “kept they are shape” is not a sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Fast-twitch muscle fibers, which make up a far larger share of an elite sprinter's calf than of a marathoner's, can generate force several times faster than the slow-twitch type, yet within seconds of a race's start the bulk of ______ power is gone. The cause is chemical: phosphocreatine, the compound these fibers burn first, is nearly exhausted after about ten seconds of all-out effort.
explanation: The power that disappears belongs to the subject of the sentence, “fast-twitch muscle fibers.” The next sentence confirms it: the fuel runs out in “these fibers.” Fibers is plural, so the possessive determiner has to be “their.” Every singular noun near the blank is a decoy: the sprinter's calf, the marathoner's, the slow-twitch type, and a race's start.

A.why: You paired the pronoun with a nearby singular noun. The likeliest is “the slow-twitch type,” which also contradicts the passage, since that fiber type is not the one losing power. The antecedent is the plural “fibers.”

C.why: “It's” means “it is.” That puts a verb inside the noun phrase “the bulk of ___ power,” and it is singular when the antecedent is plural.

D.why: You saw that the antecedent is plural but chose the contraction. “They're” means “they are,” and “the bulk of they are power” makes no sense.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The contour lines on a topographic map, which a novice reader can mistake for a tangle of hiking trails or for one long winding road, never cross. Each of ______ marks a single elevation, and no spot on the ground can sit at two heights at once.
explanation: The blank refers to “the contour lines,” the plural subject of the previous sentence. The relative clause in between is full of singular nouns: a reader, a tangle, one road. Next, look at the pronoun's job. It is the object of the preposition “of,” so it needs the object form. The plural object pronoun is “them,” which gives “Each of them marks a single elevation.”

A.why: You matched the pronoun to a singular noun near it, such as the map or the road. The lines mark elevations, so the antecedent is the plural “contour lines.”

B.why: You found the right plural antecedent but stopped there. After the preposition “of” you need the object form. “Each of they” is ungrammatical.

D.why: “Its” is a possessive determiner, so it turns “marks” into a noun (“its marks”). The sentence is then left with no main verb. It is also singular, and the antecedent is plural.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Japanese has absorbed thousands of words from Portuguese, Dutch, and English over roughly five centuries, but borrowed words rarely arrive intact. Because ______ sound system allows almost no clusters of consonants, a loan such as the English “strike” is broken up with inserted vowels and enters the language as sutoraiku, pronounced in five beats rather than one.
explanation: The sound system that breaks up consonant clusters belongs to the language doing the borrowing, which is Japanese. The sentence calls it “the language” at the end. Japanese is one language and a thing, so you need the singular possessive determiner “its.” Note that the plural noun right before the blank, “borrowed words,” is the subject of a different clause.

B.why: You matched the pronoun to “borrowed words” or to the three source languages. Words don't have sound systems. And English plainly allows clusters like “str,” so that reading also contradicts the passage.

C.why: You picked the right referent but the contraction. “Because it is sound system allows…” has a verb where a possessive belongs.

D.why: “They're” means “they are,” so it creates a verb where a possessive belongs. It is also plural, while the antecedent, Japanese, is singular.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The hundreds of recorded Cinderella tales, from the ninth-century Chinese story of Ye Xian to the version Charles Perrault published in France in 1697, disagree on nearly every detail, from the helper who aids the heroine to the fate of her stepsisters. Yet ______ heroines are almost always recognized by an object that fits no one else.
explanation: The heroines belong to the tales. The head of the first sentence's subject is “the hundreds of recorded Cinderella tales,” which is plural, and the verb “disagree” agrees with it. So the possessive determiner has to be the plural “their.” The plural noun “heroines” right after the blank confirms it. Each tale has its own heroine, and all of them together are what “their” covers.

A.why: You matched the pronoun to a singular noun inside the long interrupter, such as “the story” or “the version.” Those are examples tucked between the subject and its verb. The subject itself is plural.

B.why: You were pulled by “the heroine” and “her stepsisters” just before the blank. A heroine cannot have “heroines.” The pronoun has to name what owns them, which is the tales.

D.why: You linked the pronoun to Perrault, the only man named. He wrote one version, but the sentence is about the heroines of hundreds of tales, most of which he had nothing to do with.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Neutrophils, the most abundant white blood cells in the human body, were long described as simple eaters of bacteria. In 2004, however, researchers reported that one of these cells, when faced with more microbes than it can swallow, may instead expel ______ own DNA as a sticky web that snares the invaders outside the cell.
explanation: Strip out “researchers reported that” and the interrupting clause “when faced with more microbes than it can swallow.” What remains is “one of these cells…may instead expel ______ own DNA.” The subject is “one,” not “cells,” so it is singular, and a cell is a thing. You need the singular possessive determiner “its.”

B.why: You saw that “neutrophils,” “cells,” “microbes,” and “researchers” are all plural, and you matched one of them. The head of the subject is “one,” which is singular.

C.why: “They're” means “they are.” “Expel they are own DNA” has no grammatical sense, and it is plural when the subject is singular.

D.why: You got the number right but chose the contraction. “It's” means “it is,” and a possessive is needed before “own DNA.”

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In drypoint, the artist scratches lines directly into a copper plate with a steel needle, throwing up a ridge of metal, called a burr, along each line. The burr holds extra ink and gives drypoint lines their velvety softness, but it is fragile: a plate rarely yields more than a few dozen strong impressions before the press has flattened ______ burr.
explanation: The press flattens the burr on the plate, which is the thing that “yields” the impressions. The plate is singular and a thing, so you need the singular possessive determiner “its.” The trap is the plural noun right before the blank, “impressions.” The passage's own “their velvety softness” also gets you used to reaching for “their.”

A.why: You matched the pronoun to “impressions,” the plural noun next to the blank, or to “lines” from earlier. Paper impressions don't have a burr. The burr is raised on the plate.

B.why: “They're” means “they are.” That puts a verb where a possessive is needed, and it is plural when the antecedent, plate, is singular.

C.why: You found the singular plate but chose the contraction. “Has flattened it is burr” uses “it is” where a possessive belongs.
